morning.title: Google teams with nuclear power giant to give reactors a tune-up
morning.text: Google on Tuesday struck a deal with Constellation Energy for 3,590 megawatts of future energy supply, including nearly a gigawatt of new nuclear capacity, as the search and advertising giant tries to find enough energy to power its datacenter ambitions. The 20-year power purchase agreement will see Constellation, the largest purveyor of atomic energy in the US, bring an additional 890 megawatts of nuclear capacity online by making "targeted investments at multiple nuclear plants." We understand those investments will go toward upgrades to at least 11 existing nuclear plants across Illinois, Pennsylvania, and New Jersey through a process known as uprating. "By modernizing and upgrading turbines, steam generators, and digital control systems at operating plants, uprates deliver substantial capacity gains without the multi-year timelines or interconnection bottlenecks associated with greenfield construction," the power company explained in a statement. The other 2,700 megawatts the deal covers will come from other unspecified sources. Constellation expects to spend $4.3 billion to fulfill its side of the deal, and plans to complete its first uprated reactor by 2028. Google is on track to spend as much as $205 billion on datacenters and compute this year, but all that money is wasted if it can't secure power to make its servers and GPUs work. The hyperscaler is far from the only one scrambling to secure adequate power to keep its AI ambitions from starving. Microsoft also tapped Constellation to reignite the Three Mile Island Unit 1 reactor – you know, the one that didn't partially melt down back in 1979. That reactor is expected to come online as early as next year. Meta is also making noise about nuclear. The Social Network is working with Constellation to save a doomed nuclear plant in Illinois. Earlier this year, Meta revealed that its nuclear and clean energy commitments now total 6.6 gigawatts, though it's worth noting that figure depends heavily on the successful rollout of small modular reactors, an unproven form of miniature nuke plant. ®

morning.title: Anthropic Claude subscription plan provides more value than OpenAI's, study says
morning.text: The rivalry between Anthropic and OpenAI, the two leading US AI model makers, is no contest when it comes to assessing which one gives you more value for your subscription money, according to industry research firm SemiAnalysis. Following changes to OpenAI's $200 per month subscription plan that effectively halved its value, SemiAnalysis looked at the various subscription plans offered by AI companies, because that's still the main way that individuals and small businesses buy AI services. AI subscriptions are heavily subsidized – customers get far more tokens for their money than they would paying metered API rates. And SemiAnalysis argues that it's necessary to delve into subscription pricing to evaluate AI shops financially because subscription usage consumes a disproportionate amount of company compute resources. Claude subscriptions, the biz claims, take up about 42 percent of Anthropic's inference compute while generating just 10 percent of its revenue. And those subscriptions provide considerable value. "Anthropic is an overwhelmingly better deal, offering ~5x the API-equivalent value across the board," SemiAnalysis claims in reference to mid-tier models GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5. "You could argue that this is unfair for [OpenAI] because 6.1 Sol is much cheaper per token than Opus 5.5, but the gap is still massive even if you switch to comparing the number of tokens." OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment. SemiAnalysis' calculation relies on measuring token output rates, converting those into tokens per 5-hour usage window and per month, and then computing the API-equivalent value. Company researchers contend that API-equivalent value is the best figure for capturing the value of a subscription plan, though they allow that other measures like raw token volume may be more appropriate in some instances. API-based comparisons can be slow to account for the rapidly shifting capabilities of models that come to market. The debut of a new open source model, for example, can alter what's possible at a given price. For those with access to subscription plans, the subsidized prices clearly offer real value, so much so that there's an underground market for reselling tokens from pooled subscription accounts in many parts of the world. But there are other ways to measure AI value. Artificial Analysis, for example, tracks cost per task – the estimated dollar cost of completing a specific task. By that yardstick, GPT-6.1 Sol ($0.72) is far more affordable than Claude Opus 5.5 ($5.98), at least for those paying API rates. But that ratio may not be true for different tasks – benchmark performance may not reflect your workload. As measured by tokens, Claude Pro ($20 per month) provides 2.9 billion tokens per month, compared to ChatGPT ($20/mo) at 1 billion tokens per month, according to SemiAnalysis. But models may use more or fewer tokens than others for the same task, and when the output is functional, like code, AI output may achieve a similar result across different models but with differing degrees of efficiency. Anticipating AI costs gets more complicated for businesses, which can't count on subscription subsidies and may not have experience with AI cost management. In a July report, McKinsey said 93 percent of enterprises exceeded their AI budgets. "I think all businesses are seeing their AI costs rise," said Dhruv Amin, co-founder of AI agent biz Skydive, in an interview with The Register. Since the beginning of the year, he said, AI has been getting better at solving certain business problems, and companies have started deploying AI more widely, then noticing their token bills going through the roof. "The labs typically subsidize their prosumer plans with subscription pricing massively," said Amin. "And I think it's part of their marketing funnel because more people are able to use the tools, get familiar with the tools, and then bring those tools to work." But for larger companies, he said, two problems arise. You have more employees than can fit on a subsidized plan and, at scale, costs add up fast. "A huge way that enterprises solve this is being able to make a workload work well on the frontier and then quickly switch it to an open source model that they control and that they can serve at a much lower fraction of the cost," he said. "And so for us internally we were able to drop our AI costs 75 percent plus just by moving them all to Skydive Glide, which is our model router that for the given workload tries to find an equivalent open source model that can handle that workload without a quality drop. And so today we run a lot of our workloads on GLM-5.3 Flash." Amin said that companies adept at AI cost management maintain evaluation benchmarks that reflect their workloads. OpenAI will begin automatically watermarking text generated with ChatGPT in the European Union, the company has announced. It will also offer the watermarking feature in other regions, but it will be off by default outside of the EU.

The move in Europe is driven by a need to comply with the EU AI Act, which took effect in August. It requires marking content produced by AI models in a way that another tool can detect. Unfortunately, there is still no completely effective and reliable way to do that. A few standards already exist, like SynthID and the C2PA project, but they are relatively easy to circumvent for anyone with basic know-how.

The same is likely true for OpenAI's watermark. Its method is proprietary; the company calls it textGrain, and has published a technical paper explaining how it works. But in general, it works like other LLM watermarking tools we've seen in the past: It puts patterns in the word choices that are not clear to a human reader, and that don't meaningfully change the general quality of the output, but that someone with a key can use a specialized detector to find. morning.title: Permanent daylight saving time could be a public health time bomb
morning.text: President Trump is pushing hard for the US Senate to make daylight saving time permanent so, among other things, golfers can stay on the course longer, but it may not be such a bright idea. New research out of Canada suggests that, even if Americans would get an extra hour of daylight in the evening, the ill health effects of permanent daylight saving time could outweigh the benefits. A paper published in the Canadian Medical Association Journal on Monday reviewed evidence on the health effects of permanent daylight saving time (pDST) as several Canadian jurisdictions move to stop changing their clocks. It finds that the opposite approach - adoption of permanent standard time (pST) - would actually be better for people’s health. Sorry, night owls and after-work social butterflies, but the science simply isn’t with you on this one. “Permanent DST preserves later evening light that may facilitate commuting, recreation, social participation, and some economic activity, but it also prolongs darkness on winter mornings,” the authors note. Prolonged morning darkness doesn't really jibe with the inner workings of the human body and light’s essential role in regulating the circadian rhythm. Sure, no one wants to drive home from work in the dark, but we really need morning light to get us functioning properly. Our circadian rhythms, the authors explain, actually run on a slightly longer schedule than a full day - 24.2 hours. For that reason, we rely on natural sunlight to keep us synchronized with the world around us. Morning light is some of the most important, the authors note, because it jump starts that rhythm, wakes us up and gets us moving. Evening light, on the other hand, delays the circadian rhythm, messing with our sense of “social time” and making it tougher to get to sleep and wake up rested in the morning. The effects of later evening light can show up in sleep, mood, education, and work productivity, the authors noted, and we don’t even need pDST to see some of those associations - we can just look at time zones. Move from east to west in the US or Canada and you’ll get some considerable differences in when the sun rises and sets in a particular time zone - in some cases, sunrise and sunset can differ by more than an hour of clock time across a single time zone. In one study cited by the Canadian analysis, residents on the western side of US time zones, where the sun sets later, got around an hour less sleep a week. The study also estimated that an additional hour of sleep per week was associated with around 5 percent higher long-term earnings. Similar results turned up in a German study, the team noted. Another study found that workers on the western end of US time zones ended up working fewer hours, too. On the educational front, an extra hour of sunlight before school was associated with higher math and reading scores in a Florida study “comparable in magnitude to meaningful class-size reductions.” “Ending biannual clock adjustments may eliminate transition harms that last a few weeks, but the health effects of permanent time are likely to be chronic,” the authors noted. “The preponderance of health evidence favors pST, which would align with the recommendations of sleep and chronobiology societies worldwide.” This isn’t the first time researchers have concluded such. British sleep scientists concluded much the same in 2024, which led to their recommendation to permanently kill DST in favor of a permanent shift to Greenwich Mean Time. That isn’t stopping the US from plowing ahead with plans for pDST, though. The Senate passed a measure to enshrine DST in 2022, but the House never acted on it. This time around, the House has passed its own bill to enact pDST, but the Senate is dithering, leading President Trump to go so far as to post the personal cellphone number of one Republican holdout on social media, Senator Tom Cotton (R-AR), who is opposed to the measure. “No one likes changing the clock, me included, but Congress has enacted permanent Daylight Savings Time multiple times before and repealed it each time once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter,” Cotton explained in a post on X following Trump’s doxxing. He’s right, too: The US has twice enacted pDST - once during World War II, which ended after the war, and again in 1973 as an energy saving measure. Congress curtailed the experiment later in 1974 following public backlash over dark winter mornings. The US isn’t alone in trying and failing at enacting pDST, either, as the Canadian paper points out. Russia adopted pDST in 2011 and reversed it in 2014. Chile tried and reversed it as well. In those cases, the reasons for reversing course varied, but concerns included dark winter mornings, disrupted sleep and body clocks, safety, and public dissatisfaction. It’s unclear whether the US government’s latest attempt at enacting pDST will succeed despite political resistance and scientific evidence that it’s a bad idea, but the researchers sure seem to hope not: They note that, if the US makes such a change, Canada will likely be pressured to conform. At the end of the day, we might all be better off just dealing with a couple of clock changes and some short-term sleep disruption. ®

Hackers obtain counterfeit TLS certificates for Google and other large services
morning.text:
Attackers hijacked three top-level domains and used their control to mint counterfeit TLS certificates for Google and other large organizations, Google said Tuesday.

The attackers launched a series of attacks on the .gh, .sl, and .as country code top-level domains (ccTLDs) and then modified authoritative DNS records for selected domains within those namespaces. By controlling those DNS records, the attackers were able to pass automated domain control validation checks and obtain unauthorized certificates for “several Google domains” and “several leading global brands and widely used online services.” Google said it updated Chrome to block all certificates it identified as unauthorized, and worked with the issuing certification authorities to ensure the unauthorized certificates for Google properties were revoked.

Certificate issuance: The weak link in the chain

TLS certificates are the cryptographic credentials that underpin authentication and encryption protections for websites, mail servers, and other Internet infrastructure. These x.509 certificates use a digital signature to bind a domain name such as google.com to a public key. The public key is publicly available, while the private key is held only by the website operator. When a connection shows that the keys match, the visiting party knows it’s connected to the authentic site rather than an impostor. Possession of unauthorized certificates allows attackers to cryptographically impersonate the affected infrastructure.

morning.title: European AI flag bearer Mistral's new open weights model is 'Le Chonk'
morning.text: Another week brings yet another open weights model and this one is huge — or at least it is for Europe's AI flag bearer Mistral, which has taken to calling the 1 trillion-parameter large language model (LLM) Le Chonk. Its product name is Mistral Large 4, which is a lot less fun than the cat-meme-inspired "very official" moniker Le Chonk. Nonetheless, the LLM is the French model-dev's biggest open weights release ever. At a trillion parameters, Le Chonk is squarely in frontier territory, and like most modern frontier models, it is multimodal, reasoning, and employs a mixture of experts (MoE) architecture with about 49 billion active parameters to keep serving costs low. Mistral didn't offer any guidance on hardware requirements in its release blog, but the model is still small enough to run reasonably on 8-way GPU boxes like Nvidia's HGX B300 or AMD's MI355X. We know far more about the hardware the model was trained on. According to Mistral, this Chonker was trained using roughly 3,800 Grace Blackwell GPUs — or around 52 NVL72 racks — in Mistral's own datacenters located in Europe on a corpus spanning more than 160 languages using a combination of supervised pre-training and reinforcement learning. Sovereign AI remains a major focus for Europe and Mistral is clearly cashing in on demand for frontier class models trained and run within Europe's borders. The model itself is currently in preview, but you won't have to wait long for its weights to drop. Mistral expects them to be live on Hugging Face and other model repos within the month. Early testing by independent benchmarking firm Artificial Analysis puts Le Chonk at a major disadvantage relative to OpenAI or Anthropic's flagship models. In the AI guru's intelligence leaderboard, Mistral Large 4 preview sits between DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and OpenAI's entry-level GPT6 Luna models. Having said that, Mistral's latest model outshines the United States' most capable open weights model, Thinking Machines Lab's Inkling, by a significant margin. So when it comes to non-Chinese LLMs you can actually download, Mistral does quite well. As you'd expect, Mistral's own benchmarks tell a far rosier story. Across coding, agentic, finance, and legal benchmarks, the model build shows its latest LLM trading blows with some of the top Chinese offerings from Alibaba, Moonshot, Z.AI, and DeepSeek. You can find their charts here, but as always take them with a grain of salt. One area Mistral is particularly proud of is Le Chonk's performance in cybersecurity workloads. The company claims the model is one of the strongest performers in cybersecurity benchmarks like Artificial Analysis' new Cyber index. This is a dig at proprietary American models from the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic, which have a tendency to refuse cybersecurity-related tasks that could be perceived as adversarial. As we previously reported, this is potentially problematic for customers trying to use AI models to red-team their own systems in order to identify vulnerabilities before someone else finds them. "Provider-level refusals can block legitimate vulnerability research and incident response, and where losing access to a capability mid-incident can itself become a critical security risk. ML4 pairs top-tier cyber performance with open weights and self-deployment, giving organizations both the capability and the autonomy to run advanced security work under their own policies," Mistral wrote in a blog post. According to Mistral, Le Chonk is only the first in a series of new models made possible by its €3 billion (about $3.4 billion) Series D funding round last month. The company already expects the model's performance to improve meaningfully as it continues applying reinforcement learning, which suggests a more potent Mistral Large 4.1 could be around the corner. If you'd like to give the model a spin before its weights drop later this month, it's currently available via Mistral's API. ®

morning.text:
When Ars launched in 1998, there was one way to read it: in a web browser on a PC (or Mac). Your screen of choice was either some massive CRT or a very expensive LCD monitor (or, in my case, the less-expensive grayscale, passive-matrix LCD on a PowerBook). morning.title: Wikimedia Foundation comes forward as latest OpenAI agent assault victim
morning.text: Wikipedia’s parent organization says that OpenAI agents edited some non-public wiki pages and generated traffic that may have contributed to a partial Wikidata outage in May. This makes the non-profit just the latest victim of OpenAI agents gone rogue. The Wikimedia Foundation’s chief product and technology officer Selena Deckelmann reported several “rogue agent activities” that the foundation had identified across its various open platforms. While there was no evidence OpenAI agents compromised Wikimedia systems or data, the foundation identified several unauthorized activities it believes involved agents operated by OpenAI. “The unauthorized bot activities included edits to our wikis, some unsuccessful attempts to exploit a public note-taking tool we host, and heavy traffic,” Deckelmann said. Reports of OpenAI agents going rogue and abusing websites and services have been ongoing for months, with revelations regularly emerging since the initial Hugging Face incident was made public in July. OpenAI has been cagey about admitting how many times its AIs broke out of supposedly contained environments, but every time the news cycle refresh button gets hit, more accounts emerge, with victims including foreign government agencies and even the United Nations. The company says it paused some of its training efforts, but since then it's disclosed that more than 100 organizations were notified about potentially problematic activity by its rogue AI agents. It’s not clear whether Wikimedia was among those notified; the foundation says it discovered the OpenAI intrusions as a result of its own investigation. The wiki edits weren’t made to public-facing pages, Deckelmann said, with "almost all" made to sandbox pages. That said, Wikimedia also noted that some edits were made to its citation tool, “which we believe were potentially malicious edits that were intended to misuse this tool as a proxy for fetching data from remote services.” That would be in line with some of the other activity that rogue OpenAI agents have gotten up to in some of the other recent reports of AI malfeasance. Deckelmann noted that none of the OpenAI agents it detected making these sorts of changes bothered to seek approval for the changes as required under Wikipedia bot editing policies. The OpenAI agents also attempted to exploit Wikimedia’s public Etherpad instance. Again, the agents were trying to use the tool to fetch data from other websites. Agents abusing the service also used Etherpad to take notes about their tasks, though Wikimedia doesn’t believe any coordinated effort emerged from those notes. As for the partial outage in May, Wikimedia said “millions of automated requests” hammered its public API and made hundreds of thousands of queries to the Wikidata Query Service, traffic that it believes may have contributed to the disruption. The end result for a nonprofit, volunteer-driven project like the Wikimedia Foundation, Deckelmann said, is that it makes things damn near impossible to manage. “Wikimedia’s volunteers are the ones who come in first contact with, and clean up the mess left behind by AI agents,” the Wikimedia tech boss explained, adding that the foundation’s sites and services have seen a 50 percent increase in bandwidth usage due to bot activity since 2024. “This intense pressure on our infrastructure not only adds costs for servers and humans, but if left unaddressed, can block human visitors by overloading systems and causing outages,” Deckelmann added. “We are already paying for costs that come with the increased activity.” Like other organizations that have encountered unwanted activity from OpenAI’s agents, Wikimedia believes the AI company needs to be held accountable. “While OpenAI admits to agents behaving ‘unpredictably,’ they must also acknowledge their responsibility to monitor and prevent these risks,” Deckelmann said. “AI companies are not doing enough to secure their systems and protect the public from the harm they cause.” That responsibility, she said, is that those downrange of OpenAI’s lack of accountability are the ones having to carry that burden. It’s getting harder to deal with, Deckelmann noted in a LinkedIn post, because such traffic is increasingly hard to investigate and attribute. She calls in the announcement for AI operators to be required to mark their traffic with identifiers that make attribution of bad actions easier. “Our goal with the blog is to more openly discuss our vulnerability to this kind of activity and the need for more accountable actions to address it, while sharing with our volunteers and the public about the consequences,” Deckelmann said on LinkedIn. OpenAI didn't respond to questions for this story. ®

morning.text:
New Delhi: Air Marshal Ashutosh Dixit, Vice-Chief of the Indian Air Force (IAF), will take over as the next Chief of the Air Staff on 31 October.
He will assume command of the IAF from Air Chief Marshal A.P.Singh who will superannuate that day.
An Experimental Test Pilot and Qualified Flying Instructor with more than 3,500 hours of flying experience, Dixit will be the first officer to have commanded a Mirage-2000 squadron to go on to become the IAF chief.
His appointment is significant as he belongs to a generation of fighter pilots that came of age with the induction of the Mirage-2000 into the IAF and the evolution of modern air warfare, including beyond-visual-range (BVR) combat. The warfighting is now increasingly about beyond visual range tactics and capabilities.
Dixit was commissioned into the IAF’s fighter stream on 6 December 1986. He is an alumnus of the National Defence Academy, the Defence Staff Services College in Bangladesh, and the National Defence College.
A keen observer of the changing nature of aerial warfare, Dixit has spoken candidly about the growing role of unmanned systems and their integration with manned aircraft.
In May, while serving as the Chief of Integrated Defence Staff (CISC), Dixit said that the robotic warfare of the future was already here and that unmanned aerial systems were no longer merely enablers but means of warfare in their own right.
Unmanned aircraft were “already replacing manned aircraft in an increasing variety of roles” and were influencing the outcome of conflicts, he asserted.
Apart from the Mirage-2000, Dixit has extensive flying experience on a range of aircraft, including the Mirage-2000, various MiG variants, HPT-32, An-32, Avro, Kiran, Jaguar, IL-78, Hawk and Tejas.
During his nearly four-decade career, he has been involved in several operations and exercises, including Operation Safed Sagar, Operation Rakshak, Cope India and Operation Sindoor.
As Commanding Officer, Dixit re-equipped No. 9 Squadron with the Mirage-2000 and later commanded a frontline fighter air base in the Western Sector as well as a premier fighter training base in the Southern Sector. He has also served as Directing Staff at the Air Force Test Pilots School and as Principal Director, Air Staff Requirement, at Air Headquarters.
Dixit subsequently served as Air Defence Commander of Southern Air Command and held key appointments including Assistant Chief of the Air Staff (Projects), Assistant Chief of the Air Staff (Plans), Senior Air Staff Officer at Headquarters South Western Air Command and Deputy Chief of the Air Staff at Air Headquarters.
As CISC, Dixit pushed for greater jointness and integration among the three services. During his tenure, multiple joint doctrines and orders were issued and several initiatives were undertaken to strengthen the armed forces’ capabilities across domains.

morning.text:
Hyderabad: Defence Minister Rajnath Singh Tuesday commissioned the first of the five indigenous Fleet Support Ships (FSS-1), Surya, at Hindustan Shipyard Limited (HSL) in Visakhapatnam, marking a critical evolutionary step in the Navy’s operational reach across the Indian Ocean Region (IOR).
The vessel was built with one clear role: to replenish frontline warships at sea with fuel, water, ammunition, and other essential stores, to bolster naval endurance. It fundamentally increases the Navy’s capacity to fight longer and harder at sea without returning to port, Chief of the Naval Staff, Admiral Krishna Swaminathan said, during the launch.
With a displacement of approximately 43,500 tonnes DWT (deadweight tonnage), Surya entered the water of the Bay of Bengal at Vizag just 18 months after steel cutting, a feat for the once-bootstrapped Hindustan Shipyard Limited. Steel cutting marks the official beginning of the shipbuilding lifecycle.
HSL has been commissioned and contracted by the Navy to build five Fleet Support Ships at a cost of Rs 19,500 crore, a Press Bureau of India statement said.
Launched the first indigenous Fleet Support Ship ‘INS Surya’ at Hindustan Shipyard Ltd in Visakhapatnam. The launch of FSS1 is a symbol of achievement, keel laying of FSS5 is a symbol of resolve and the new Slipway is a symbol of our growing capability. HSL is fast emerging as a… pic.twitter.com/xH3kfJHOEm
— Rajnath Singh (@rajnathsingh) October 6, 2026
Built to defend herself and support warships in replenishing themselves, Surya also has a helicopter deck that can accommodate multi-role helicopters. Her fit includes AK 630 guns, the Kavach decoy system, the marines torpedo defence system, and electronic warfare suites named Shakti, and Sea King 42 Charlie helicopters. Surya is a large vessel—223.6 metres long and 31.5 metres wide—equipped with two main engines of 2 MW each to help her sail at a top speed of 20 knots, according to details provided by HSL at the time of launch.
According to the PIB statement, the launch of the FSS-1 was coupled with the inauguration of a 300-tonne Goliath Crane and lengthened Slipway-4, which would not just assist HSL in larger constructions, but also cement the public sector undertaking (PSU) as a premier tier-one defence shipbuilder.
Speaking at the launch of the FSS-1, the defence minister applauded the transformation of Hindustan Shipyard from a financially distressed unit to an operationally functional Category-I Miniratna PSU.
“In 2025, we categorised Hindustan Shipyard as a Miniratna PSU and ensured it was financially restored. Today, HSL is part of an Integrated National Maritime Ecosystem, being part of the Eastern Naval Command, the Naval Dockyard, and the Visakhapatnam Port. As part of India’s maritime Vision 2030, I would like Hindustan Shipyard to team up with DRDO, Academia, industry, MSMEs, and start-ups to work together as an integrated team,” Rajnath Singh said.
The 85-year-old HSL was burdened by decades of negative net worth and operational inefficiencies dating back to the 1980s. For decades, it suffered from limited naval order flows and execution delays after shifting to the Ministry of Defence (MoD) in 2010.
However, after a sustained financial bailout from the Centre, HSL turned out financially and operationally, finally tripling its turnover in FY 2024, recording sales of Rs 1,400 crore from just about Rs 478 crore in FY21. In the last few years, the PSU was able to scale its order books significantly past Rs 20,000 crore, propelled by major projects like the Navy Fleet Support Ships. Earlier in August, HSL delivered the Navy-commissioned INS Nipun, the second indigenous Nistar-class Diving Support Vessel (DSV).
Admiral Krishna Swaminathan, Chief of the Naval Staff, said the FSS was critical for the Navy’s Blue Water Fleet. “It grants us three operational advantages: longer endurance, greater reach, and faster response in the Indian Ocean Region (IOR). These vessels will also be useful in humanitarian assistance, disaster relief, personnel evacuation, and help us respond in other emergencies.”
The vessel sails with a complement of 215 personnel and can carry about 20,000 tonnes of diesel, 2,500 tonnes of aviation fuel, and about 1,000 tonnes of fresh water for transfer to other ships at sea. It is equipped to also carry solid stores of provisions and coal, amounting to nearly 240 tonnes, HSL officials said during the launch.
The Chairman & Managing Director (CMD) of HSL, Rear Admiral C. Raghuram, VSM (Retd.), highlighted the historic nature of achieving three massive shipyard milestones simultaneously. At the launch of FSS-1, he said, “Two warships commissioned, a record year, and now three milestones in a single day,” referring to INS Nipun, the FSS-1, and the launch of the Goliath crane and the Slipway-4.
Rear Admiral Raghuram took over as CMD of Hindustan Shipyard Limited in July to help steer and expand HSL’s submarine and warship manufacturing capabilities.
HSL was established in 1941 as Scindia Shipyard by Walchand Hirachand in Visakhapatnam, with the foundation stone laid by Dr Rajendra Prasad, who later became India’s first President. Even before it was incorporated as a public limited company in 1951, the shipyard built Jal Usha, the country’s first modern ocean-going steamship built completely in independent India.
Later, in 1961, it was nationalised by the Indian government and renamed Hindustan Shipyard Limited.
(Edited by Amrtansh Arora)

morning.title: Asim Munir reshuffles his Corps Commanders. But three-star generals rarely leave the system in Pakistan
morning.text:
New Delhi: The Pakistan Army has reshuffled its senior command structure with the elevation of several Major Generals to Lieutenant Generals while also making new appointments to key Corps Commander-level positions.
This was made public immediately after the 277th Corps Commanders’ conference held in Rawalpindi on 2 October.
Analysts are looking at potential ramifications on Pakistan’s internal political and security landscape and the Pakistan Army’s posture vis-a-vis India. Most appointments, however, are routine.
That Field Marshal Asim Munir has picked officers based on his preference is not surprising; every Army Chief strives to do the same.
Munir’s Corps Commanders
For 11 Corps, Peshawar, Mohammed Naeem Akhtar from the Azad Kashmir Regiment has been selected. He has replaced Lt Gen Omar Ahmed Bukhari, 22 Baloch Regiment, who has now been given the post of Chief of General Staff, a highly coveted post after the Chief of the Army Staff (COAS).
The Peshawar-based XI corps is closely watched, for it is not only among the army’s key field formations, but those heading it typically assume a bigger public role. It also sees a greater degree of activity, liaisons more closely with the ISI, and has a larger footprint in civilian affairs since its commander sits on Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s Provincial Apex Committee. The logic, hence, goes that those who are selected to head this corps are tapped for bigger roles in the future.
Umar Bashir, Artillery, has been made Corps Commander, 4 Corps, Lahore, by Field Marshal Asim Munir.
Field Marshal Asim Munir has appointed Lt Gen Shakirullah Khattak, Armoured Corps (13 Lancers) who was chairman, Heavy Industries, Taxila, the new Corps Commander at Mangla, or the I Corps. This follows a recent convention of sending either armoured corps or artillery officers there.
Khattak will be replacing Lt Gen Nauman Zakaria, who was also an Armoured Corps officer. While being the commander of I corps, Zakaria was simultaneously heading the newly established Army Rocket Force Command (ARFC), announced by Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif in August 2025. He captured headlines at this year’s Shangri-La Dialogue in Singapore in May. Though he leaves the I Corps, there has been no reported change of guard for the ARFC.
The Mangla Corps deals with Pakistan’s eastern border—India. It has historically had three Infantry divisions, and one Armoured Division under it, positioned at Jhelum, Kharian and Mangla.
Rana Banerji, who headed the Pakistan desk at R&AW, in a monograph dated September 2013 writes: “After the 2003 ceasefire on the Line of Control (LOC), one of these divisions was temporarily deployed to the Western sector, to assist XI Corps, Peshawar in counter-insurgency (COIN) operations against tribal insurgencies in Swat and FATA.” Presently, the Mangla Corps retains its armoured components alongside infantry and mechanised infantry divisions.
Field Marshal Asim Munir has appointed Mohammad Amer Najam, 19 Sind Regiment, who was serving as inspector general, training and evaluation at General Headquarters, as corps commander, 2 Corps, Multan. The I Corps Mangla, along with II Corps Multan, forms the Pakistan Army’s Strike Corps.
Lieutenant General Inayat Hussain, Frontier Force Regiment, hitherto chief of logistics staff at GHQ, has been appointed the new corps commander, 12 Corps, Quetta by Field Marshal Asim Munir.
Among three-star appointments, including at the corps-commander level, the Army Chief strives for ensuring representation from all major arms (Armoured Corps, Infantry, Artillery, Engineers, Air Defence) to maintain institutional equity and cohesion across the service.
Three-star ranks never retire
According to Rana Banerji’s column for Rediff, at least six lieutenant generals of the 80th Pakistan Military Academy long courses, who were due for retirement after completing four years in this rank, may now be phased out.
These include Lt Gen Inam Haider Malik (Engineers, Chairman, National Disaster Management Authority) and Lt Gen Fayyaz Hussain Shah (Sind Regiment, Corps Commander, 4 Corps, Lahore); Lt Gen Muhammad Zafar Iqbal (Air Defence, commander, Air Defence Command, Rawalpindi); Lt Gen Shahid Imtiaz (Azad Kashmir Regiment, Military Secretary); Lt Gen Ahsan Gulrez (Frontier Force Regiment, Corps Commander, 2 Corps, Multan) and Lt Gen Nauman Zakaria (Armoured Corps, Corps Commander, 1 Corps, Mangla).
Formally, three-star generals in Pakistan do retire. In practice, retirement doesn’t equal being out of the army’s orbit. They only move out of General Headquarters (GHQ), Rawalpindi, into positions that the high command at GHQ continues to shape.
Take the example of Lt General Nauman Mahmood (Retd), who was appointed as the first secretary general of the Makkah Defence Alliance in September 2026. He had notably commanded the XI Corps, Peshawar and his tenure had coincided with one of the most sensitive periods along Pakistan’s western border, witnessing the withdrawal of the United States from Afghanistan.
A 2018 study by Paul Staniland et al., shows that retired corps commanders rarely enter electoral politics. There is an “institutionalised transmission belt that shifts retired elites into military-owned charitable foundations and affiliated corporations, posts in the civilian government, and other positions of real and/or symbolic authority”.
These positions, labeled “off-ramps”, provide officers strong incentives to toe the organisational line while serving and to avoid directly participating in politics after retirement, the study adds. More so as for most of the Pakistani military elite, their first corps command is their last major command.
There’s the Water and Power Development Authority (WAPDA) that is chaired by a retired Lt Gen—Muhammad Saeed—who had earlier served as the CGS and corps commander of 5-Corps Karachi. Even Pakistan’s National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) has more or less been headed by a three-star level officer.
However, the dominant post-retirement slot is a blend of foundations and associated corporations led by the military—and for the military, such as the Fauji Foundation and its subsidiaries, Army Welfare Trust and Defence Housing Authority.
Ayesha Siddiqa, in her seminal work Military Inc., termed the military’s deep penetration into Pakistan’s economy as ‘Milbus’ (Military-Business).
Fauji Foundation is headed by a retired lieutenant general—Anwar Ali Hyder. The governing body of the Defence Housing Authority (DHA) is chaired by Lt Gen Muhammad Ali (Retd) who is also the Secretary Defence, Ministry of Defence. DHA acquires land for real estate purposes to provide premier housing to the military fraternity, which has resulted in the army being known as Pakistan’s “biggest land grabber”.
The post-retirement trajectory of three-star generals reinforces that Pakistan is not a state with an army, but rather its army has a state to itself.
Pakistan’s intelligence chiefs
Last month, ThePrint reported on the Pakistan Army carrying out a series of new appointments at the two-star level. Most notable was a change in command of Director General-Military Intelligence (DG-MI), now assigned to Major General Adil Iftikhar Warraich.
This post matters because it is a stepping stone, given the convention of DG-MI ascending to the head of ISI. Take the example of the incumbent army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, who served as the head of MI and ISI both, later bagging the biggest post of army chief.
If DG-MI’s appointment was noteworthy last month, then the one-year extension given to the DG ISI (Inter-Services Intelligence)—Lt Gen Asim Malik—who has been serving the post since September 2024 stands out.
(Edited by Viny Mishra)

morning.title: C-130J-30 vs C-390: Lockheed lays out its case for India’s medium transport aircraft deal
morning.text:
New Delhi: Drawing from India’s experience of its fleet of the C-130J-30 Super Hercules, Lockheed Martin has sharpened its pitch saying the aircraft offers far greater usable capacity and operational flexibility than its nearest competitor—Brazil’s Embraer C-390 Millennium for the mega Medium Transport Aircraft (MTA) programme.
The American aerospace major is competing with Embraer for what is the largest military transport aircraft contract, seeking to replace the ageing AN 32s and the IL-76 operated by the IAF.
While the numbers sought by the IAF formally in a Request for Proposal sent out to Indian players is for 60 aircraft, it is expected to go up subsequently.
European aviation major Airbus has dropped out of the contest, leaving the C-130J-30 and C-390 as principal contenders.
The Request for Proposal (RFP) for the programme was issued on 12 August, with bids due by 2 December.
Lockheed is offering the latest version of the C-130J-30, known as the C-130J-30 Block 8.1.2 to the IAF with 12 aircraft to be built at its facility in Marietta, Georgia, while the remaining 48 would be manufactured in India in partnership with Tata Advanced Systems Limited (TASL). The RFP states a minimum of 40 percent indigenous content.
Speaking to ThePrint, Robert Toth, Vice President, Strategy & Business Development, Air Mobility and Maritime Missions at Lockheed Martin, underlined that what the IAF has and what the company is offering is the C-130J–30 and not just the C-130J that everyone believes it is.
“Many of the characteristics that get attributed to the C-130J are actually of the C-130H or the original version of the C-130J, which was a shorter version,” he said.
He said that when people say that C-130J has a capacity of 18-19 tonnes, they are wrong because the C-130J-30 that the IAF uses has a capacity of 22 tonnes.
The C-130J-30 is a stretched version of the Hercules, with the fuselage extended by about 14 feet to provide additional internal cargo space.
The difference is significant, with the IAF’s RFP stating that the aircraft should have a minimum capacity of 18 tonnes and a maximum of 30.
The Embraer aircraft has a capacity of 26 tonnes and falls in between.
‘It’s about volume, not weight’
One of Toth’s central arguments is that maximum payload weight alone does not determine the effectiveness of a tactical transport aircraft.
He argued that in most logistics missions, the aircraft runs out of available cargo volume before reaching their maximum payload weight.
“When you think about moving cargo, it is really a math problem, the amount of items you need to move over a specific period of time,” Toth, a former C-130J pilot with the US Air Force said.
He claimed that compared to the C-390, the C-130J-30 can carry 60 percent more passengers, 45 percent more fully combat-loaded paratroopers and 30 percent more litter positions for casualty evacuation.
He also claimed the C-130J-30 can accommodate eight standard cargo pallets compared to the seven on the C-390, a 15 percent difference.
These figures are Lockheed Martin’s own comparative claims and they did not give specific numbers.
However, the company’s website says it can carry 128 combat troops and 92 paratroopers.
Lockheed argues that the additional usable floor space of the C-130J-30 therefore matters more than a simple comparison of maximum payload figures.
The company also pointed to the aircraft’s ability to operate from short and austere runways and at high-altitude airfields.
Lockheed argues that its aircraft possess the best short-field takeoff/landing performance, highest pallet/passenger/litter capacity, lowest fuel use rate, greater range, lower carbon footprint, combat proven survivability, and best unprepared airfield capability/durability.
Toth also said that The C-130J-30 requires fewer sorties to complete combat troop deployments and humanitarian operations.
Its ability to transport more personnel and equipment with fewer sorties allows faster delivery of forces for contingency and humanitarian operations while also reducing overall operational costs, he said.
India’s experience with the Hercules
The IAF inducted its first C-130J-30 aircraft in 2010 and has since used the platform extensively for a range of operations.
Toth said the Indian fleet has accumulated around 58,000 flight hours while maintaining a availability ration of above 85 percent.
The aircraft have been used for operations ranging from disaster relief to the evacuation of Indian citizens from conflict zones.
One of the most daunting tasks that the aircraft did was landing at Daulat Beg Oldi (DBO) in Ladakh at an altitude of about 16,600 feet.
The aircraft has also been used for operations in Afghanistan and Sudan, as well as humanitarian assistance missions, including ongoing operations in Nepal.
Lockheed is placing considerable emphasis on this operational experience as it makes its case for the MTA.
The company says the global C-130J fleet has accumulated more than three million flight hours across roughly 28 operators, creating what it describes as a large pool of operational experience and feedback for continuous upgrades to the aircraft.
New aircraft more advanced than IAF’s existing C-130Js
The aircraft proposed for the MTA programme would not be identical to the C-130Js currently operated by India. The existing Indian aircraft are Block 6 configuration, while Lockheed says it intends to offer the latest Block 8.1.2 configuration for the MTA.
The newer configuration incorporates upgrades to communications, navigation, avionics and software, among other improvements, he said without getting into details.
Lockheed also says it has the capability to upgrade India’s existing 12 aircraft to the same configuration.
That upgrade, however, would be a separate contract and is not part of the current MTA proposal, he said.
Toth argued that if the upgrade is undertaken, it would allow the IAF eventually to operate a common fleet of 72 C-130J-30s, the existing 12 plus the 60 MTA aircraft, that will come with common training, maintenance and logistics infrastructure.
Four engines versus two
Another key part of Lockheed’s pitch is the C-130J’s four-engine turboprop configuration. The company argues that the configuration provides greater engine redundancy during operations in difficult environments, particularly at high-altitude and high-temperature airfields.
Its executives contrasted this with the C-390, which uses two turbofan jet engines.
The Lockheed argument is that an aircraft losing one engine can still continue its mission or complete a take-off or landing in circumstances where a twin-engine aircraft would have less redundancy.
This is being presented by Lockheed as an operational advantage, particularly given India’s geography, which ranges from sea-level environments to some of the world’s highest military airfields, he said.
Lockheed highlights Tata partnership
The company is also seeking to make its existing industrial presence in India a central part of its case. Under the MTA proposal, 48 of the 60 aircraft would be produced in India with TASL.
Lockheed says its relationship with Tata goes back more than a decade and that the two companies have already established manufacturing capabilities in India through their joint ventures.
One of these facilities in Hyderabad has produced 265 C-130J empennages, Toth underlined.
He pointed to its work on S-92 helicopter cabins and F-16 fighter wings as evidence that the industrial ecosystem required for a major aircraft production programme already exists.
Lockheed says more than 500 Indian suppliers, including around 140 MSMEs, form part of its global supply chain.
Its argument is that this existing network would allow it to scale up production for the MTA programme faster than a manufacturer starting to establish an Indian ecosystem only after winning the contract.
Lockheed is also setting up a C-130J maintenance, repair and overhaul facility in Bengaluru.
The company says the facility is on schedule to be completed by the end of 2026, with the first Indian aircraft expected to enter the facility around the first or second quarter of 2027.
(Edited by Viny Mishra)
